The Commission remains an indispensable platform to foster dialogue, build bridges, and encourage peacebuilding efforts at national and local levels to address tensions arising from political, ethnic, and regional differences. Complementing the Commission is the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund, which offers timely, catalytic, and flexible resources in support of nationally-led peacebuilding strategies that are often underfunded. Let me share three examples of how this complementarity works. In Sao Tome and Principe, the Commission's engagement created a platform among national authorities, the international community, and financial institutions grounded in a joint strategic assessment by the United Nations and the Economic Community of Central African States, ECAS. Responding swiftly to these priorities, the Peacebuilding Fund financed initiatives to strengthen access to justice, a cornerstone for inclusive governance. In Colombia, the visit of the Peacebuilding Commission in August underscored its political support to the implementation of the peace agreement. 11 years of Peacebuilding Fund investment have bolstered community resilience, restored social cohesion, and advanced inclusive governance through restorative justice initiatives and reintegration support for ex-combatants. In conclusion, we need to renew our political will and shared commitment to a better future for all, one in which no one is left behind and where peace is not merely an aspiration, but a lived reality. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Slovenia, and I will now give floor to His Excellency, Stephan Pakual, Minister of Peacebuilding of South Sudan.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to begin by thanking today's briefers for sharing their experiences and insight, which are invaluable as we collectively actively seek to advance peacebuilding and social cohesion. I also wish to express our deep gratitude to all the funders of the Peacebuilding Fund, with special thanks to Germany and Finland for their steadfast support. Your investment is an important international contribution to peacekeeping and peacebuilding in South Sudan. South Sudan is a young nation still on a journey, grappling with challenges of forging unity in our rich, multicultural society, working to develop a governance system that truly serve all our people. We are making progress, but we continue to face significant frugalities and division. As we look forward With the planned withdrawal of UNMISS, the important peace building and inclusive governance become even more critical. Our institution remain fragile and our communities is still vulnerable to the risk of relapse back into conflicts. We are also aware that climate change is compounding our challenges, more frequent floods, and drought are disrupting livelihood, fueling displacement and increasing tension among the communities. Addressing the climate-related risk must be an integral part of our peacebuilding strategy. We commend the Peacebuilding Fund for its vital investment in South Sudan, particularly in programs that promote women peace and security, and youth leading peace agenda. These initiatives are empowering women and young people to be agent of reconciliations and positive change and are helping to build bridges across our diverse communities. Let us be clear, investing in peace is far less costly than investing in war. The dividend of peace are measured not only in stability, but in the hope and opportunity it brings to our people. We urge the United Nations and the international community not to abandon South Sudan at this critical juncture. With your continued support, we are committed to working tirelessly to become a peace-building success story, a nation where diversity is the source of its strength and where every citizen can contribute to peace-building and prosperous future. Thank you very much.
Dear Minister, thank you very much. I will now give the floor to His Excellency Andreas Kravik, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, followed by Panama.

Thank you. Thank you very much, and let me start by thanking Germany for organizing this very timely meeting. The current moment in history demonstrates with frightening clarity how vital it is to invest in peacebuilding and conflict prevention. Norway has invested heavily in social cohesion, building a universal welfare state that ensures everyone a social safety net, access to quality education, and equal opportunities to get ahead in society. Doing so counteracts the resentments and hostilities systematic exclusion generates. It is conflict prevention in practice. So too globally, the UN peacebuilding architecture represents a unique approach to peace based on national ownership, collaboration rather than intervention, linking targeted development initiatives on the ground to peace. It enjoys broad cross-regional support. The ongoing peacebuilding architecture review is an important opportunity to recommit to the principles of peacebuilding. It is also an opportunity to develop the agenda further by supporting nationally owned prevention strategies and broadening the scope for peacebuilding efforts, including how Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund can assist countries as they transition from conflict to peace. We are also excited to see how the UN80 reform process can contribute to even stronger synergies between the UN's peace making, peacekeeping, and peacebuilding efforts, and more broadly, between peace, development, humanitarian efforts, and human rights. For all of us who believe in international law and multilateralism, I think it's imperative now that we coalesce around this importance of ensuring that the UN is equipped to facilitate global solutions to global problems as we continue to try to remedy some of the crises that we're seeing and the conflicts that are still ongoing. Norway remains steadfast as one of the largest contributors to the UN Peacebuilding Fund, and we are committed to continuing our active engagement in this Commission. We are also hard at work to integrate peace-building dimensions into all our efforts pertaining to peace and development. And with that, I thank you for your attention.
I thank the representative of Norway and will now give the floor to His Excellency Carlos Arturo Hoyos Boyd, Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama, followed by India.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished ministers. We thank the Federal Republic of Germany for organizing this meeting and all the speakers who preceded me. Dear colleagues, trust building is essential to ensuring coexistence and global peace. However, it has been left on the margins of global discussions while trends towards military rearmament and extremist narratives fueled by citizens' fears, dominate forums and public opinions. In a world of such polarization and uncertainty, perhaps there is nothing more important than returning to dialogue on how to focus on recovering our shared humanity. In Panama and Latin America, we suffer daily from the consequences of neglecting this crisis of trust. However, this is a global problem. Distrust among citizens and towards democratic institutions creates a vicious cycle that breeds despair and extremism, the result of which, among many others, includes the rise of organized crime. This, in turn, creates fertile ground for further forced displacement and increases discrimination and xenophobia, further dividing our communities and countries. All of this is exacerbated by climate change and the use of AI as a political weapon with impunity. That is why it's necessary to build new alliances to continue building trust among all. As members of the PBC, we participated in the Peace Architecture Review and the Berlin Ministerial Conference. These dialogues demonstrated the need to build trust through peace education, including more women, young people, civil society, and indigenous people in decision making. They are the ones who will sustain peace over time. Ministers, the road to peace can be long, but with a genuine willing to compromise and inclusiveness, peace may arrive. Colombia, although its process has not been easy, is a Latin American example of inclusiveness. We also thank Finland and Papua New Guinea for their leadership in gender and climate change, and all countries here investing in peacebuilding. We also recognize Iraq's effort to rebuild social cohesion, even after years of fighting extremism and foreign intervention, and now facing a historic crisis due to water shortages in the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. There, where human civilization and agriculture once began, we believe hope remains. Ministers and colleagues, today, 80 years after the birth of this institution, we cannot forget one thing, which is our shared humanity and dignity. Only in this way can we face together the common challenges that threaten our existence. Let us reclaim civic spaces where anyone, regardless of religion, gender, or social class, can come together and build peace. In this way, we will strengthen community cohesion and, in turn, ensure sustainable socioeconomic development. Only by listening to each other and sharing with people who are different from us will we consolidate peace together. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Panama. We will now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. C.V. George, Vice Minister of India, followed by Uruguay.

Mr. Chair, let me begin by thanking Honorable Foreign Minister of Germany and the Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission for convening this timely meeting. especially in the context of the ongoing review of the Peacebuilding Architecture 2025. India's approach to peacekeeping and peacebuilding is guided by our civilizational ethos of the world is one family that find manifestation in our collective endeavor of moving forward to achieve peace, prosperity, and progress for all. In the realm of peacebuilding, we have been a steadfast partner through demand-driven development partnerships across the global south. Our developmental assistance projects, cumulatively valued over 40 billion U.S. dollars, comprise grants, concessional loans, and capacity building, helping countries rebuild institutions and develop resilience. Today, peacebuilding faces severe challenges with the declining finances and rising conflicts. Countries in conflict settings require adequate space-time, and resources from the international community to develop resilient governance institutions that are transparent, accountable, and inclusive. We believe that resilient governance institutions, by leveraging people-centric technological advances, such as digital public infrastructure that enables safe, inclusive, and interoperable public services for citizens and businesses, can enhance accountability, transparency, and effectiveness in public service delivery. These efforts in turn foster trust among citizens and promote social cohesion and sustainable peace. Mr. Chair, against this backdrop, I would like to offer the following six points. One, peacebuilding must remain demand-driven, guided by national ownership and priorities of the host governments. The 2025 PBAR should focus on ensuring adequate support from international community to address the long-term socioeconomic development needs and priorities of the host country. Rebuilding institutions is necessary in countries emerging from conflict to consolidate peace and avoid a relapse. Two, preparation and presentation of national peacebuilding strategy should remain voluntary. We encourage developed countries to lead by example on this front. Three, no conditionalities in terms of preparation or presentation of national peacebuilding and prevention strategies be introduced in 2025 PBIR to avail financial support from Peacebuilding Fund or IFIs. Four, resident coordinators can play a significant role in strengthening strategic coherence. and extending adequate support to host governments on their national peacebuilding priorities. Five, PBC's partnership with regional and sub-regional organizations should be further deepened, leveraging their contextual strengths and local solutions to achieve sustainable peacebuilding outcomes. Finally, enhancing support for the women Peace and Security, WPS, Youth, Peace and Security, YPS, and Children and Armed Conflict agendas to advance national priorities holds the promise of building and sustaining peace. In conclusion, Chair, we reaffirm our commitment to continue engaging constructively with our partners to strengthen PBC's effectiveness and impact. I thank you.
I thank the representative of India and will now give the floor to His Excellency, Ambassador Martin Vidal, Vice Minister of Uruguay, followed by Russia.

Thank you very much, Chairman. Uruguay welcomes the organization of this ministerial debate on the 20th anniversary of the PBC. the conviction that guides our international actions, that there can be no lasting peace without development, nor sustainable development without peace. The PPC is the right forum to bring this conviction and translate it into concrete commitments, upholding international law, bringing states together as well as UN bodies, financial institutions and civil society around priorities defined by the countries and led by their leadership. An important question for us is how to strengthen social cohesion in order to prevent violence and avoid setbacks. Experience shows that strengthening policies with a territorial approach, providing quality services to the population that makes them able to participate through representation rules, binding ones, this requires representative institutions that are accountable with verifiable data and the ability to complain, and also with safe, egalitarian, and meaningful participation of women and youth, not only as the beneficiaries of policies, but also as the designers and implementers of these policies. In this framework, the PBC and the Peacebuilding Fund can provide added value supporting intercommunity cohesion in areas affected by displacement and violence in an agile way, enabling reconciliation and reintegration, as well as encouraging formal livelihoods, attention to youth, women, and minorities, strengthening territorial equity, and the building of institutions, and upholding the rule of law. What's more, it's necessary and possible to articulate this with climate challenges and violent extremism by integrating early warning systems, because, Mr. Chairman, this is another way of helping to build peace. Management of water, cross-border cooperation when it comes to dealing with illicit substances is also important with the necessary follow-up. Uruguay underscores the importance of including dimensions on peacebuilding within the mandate of peacebuilding missions as an essential step towards the building of more resilient and inclusive societies. transforming the positive impact of the personnel deployed into lasting actions during and after transition periods. We propose, therefore, moving forward to identify different operational guidance on social cohesion as good practices, metrics, and recommended institutional actions in order to identify windows of financing for the PBF aligned with these objectives in order to put them to test with the necessary public backing and synergy with the support of multilateral international benefit, uh, development banks, Uruguay reiterates its focus on human dignity, equity, and sustainable development. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Uruguay, and I will now give the floor to His Excellency Sergey Vereshchagin, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Russia.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, distinguished colleagues. Eighty years ago, when the Charter of the United Nations was adopted, the founding fathers strove to put together such a system of checks and balances that would be able to shield the world from the horrors of a new global conflict. However, armed conflicts have not evaporated, although they have are now located have become localized at the state and regional level. Each of these conflicts has its own specific root causes, and only by addressing these root causes is it possible to achieve a meaningful, sustained resolution. The main responsibility for resolving crisis situations and achieving post-conflict recovery is borne by the affected states themselves. National governments need to seek political, diplomatic ways to extricate themselves from crises, to determine peacebuilding priorities, and to take decisions on the need or bringing in international assistance. The core principles for peacekeeping are enshrined in Security Council resolutions 1645 and 2282. which established the Peacebuilding Commission. This is a unique intergovernmental consultative body where all interested players have an opportunity to exchange views and to put forward collective recommendations to address situations in any given country. Many states who have been affected by crises, especially states in Africa, remain affected by the consequences of their colonialist past as a result of these tragic events. The natural historic process of state building was disrupted. The artificial borders were drawn up, and many peoples were divided or were put together in state bodies. In this way, the colonialist past is Africa's common root cause of conflict. The development of the situation in the Sahel-Sahara region clearly attests to the perniciousness of a reckless intervention in domestic affairs of states, first and foremost in Libya. and attempts to resolve matters through economic and political pressure. It is no coincidence that members of the Alliance of Sahel States, who are at the frontline in counterterrorism, have drawn lessons from the history of reliance on external donors and are now emphasizing the need to strengthen cooperation among themselves and to focus on the interests of their own population. Turning to Iraq. We cannot but note the success of the Iraqi government in buttressing its sovereignty, normalizing civilian life, and ensuring economic and social recovery. The measures that have been adopted by the government have helped to achieve remarkable reduction in terrorist activity. We hope that all national political forces will continue to demonstrate a responsible approach and strive to resolve disputes purely through wide-ranging dialogue for the benefit of all population groups. In light of this year's Peacebuilding Architecture Review, we should like to assure you that the Russian delegation will proactively fully participate in work on the draft resolution. This document needs to be constructive in nature and needs to fully take into account the approaches of all Member States. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the representative of Russia and give now the floor to His Excellency Leon Kaku Adom, Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Integration and Ivorians Abroad of Cote d'Ivoire.

Thank you, Chairman. My delegation is delighted to participate in this important ministerial meeting of the Peacebuilding Commission. And Cote d'Ivoire is aware of the fundamental support role to upholding peace and stability across the world that this body plays, not only thanks to the close cooperation that we have had with this body, but also because we will remember recently in 2018 and 2019, when we were a member of the Security Council. I wish also to underscore really how relevant the theme that we're dealing with and experience has shown that social cohesion, inclusive governance and the resilience of communities and building lasting peace are for and that they're intrinsically linked concepts. Indeed through solid interpersonal relations and vision of common well-being and equality as well as trust in national institutions promoting social cohesion this creates societies that are more able to build a peaceful future and makes them also more resilient inclusive governance strengthens social cohesion and enables the emergence of a sense of belonging and a collective commitment by encouraging participation of all citizens. These dynamics also are a true driving force and a cornerstone to build a strong peace that is accepted by everyone. This interaction is also verified in the processes of building and building a lasting peace in Cote d'Ivoire, the government has implemented different strategies and initiatives that illustrate this, and these are focused around the fight against poverty and social vulnerability, the promotion of the rule of law, human rights, and democratic governance, national reconciliation and political dialogue, seeking to create a peaceful social climate, raising awareness among the population as to a culture of peace, dialogue, and tolerance, strengthening the participation of women and youth as to the consolidation of peace, and decision-making processes. What's more, due to the fragilities that we see in the West African region linked to security challenges, instability, risks of cross-border and intercommunity tensions, a regional dynamic, and we are looking at better understanding and anticipating risks and strengthening confidence and trust and collaboration with neighbouring countries. These actions are engaged in through governmental bodies and their central administrations, in particular the Ministry for Social Cohesion, Solidarity and Fighting Poverty, tasked with the implementation of the policy to reduce inequalities and to improve access to basic social services. An observatory for solidarity and social cohesion has also been set up as a institution that monitors and provides warnings. Similarly, local mechanisms geared towards the prevention and settlement of conflicts do exist, in particular the peace committees and the committees for awareness raising and oversight. Civil society organizations as well as local actors, including traditional chiefs and religious leaders, are also intervening in the process, playing an important role. The Ivorian government intends to continue its coordination with all of these partners, in particular the PBC. Thank you for your kind attention.

I thank you, representative of Cote d'Ivoire, and will now give the floor to His Excellency Dr. Mohammed bin Abdulaziz Al-Kulaifi, Minister of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Qatar, followed by Austria.

Sayid Ra'is.

Mr. Chair, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Qatar expresses its gratitude to you for successfully holding this important ministerial meeting. We welcome the latest Secretary-General report on peacebuilding and sustaining peace. We thank the briefers for their valuable interventions. Mr. Chair, the State of Qatar is making tireless efforts to enhance social cohesion and inclusive governance through national development strategies and societal initiatives and international efforts. The main framework for all these efforts is the National Vision 2030, which is implemented through different national initiatives. Domestic initiatives aim to improving the quality of life, enhancing social cohesion and ensuring diversity in society. Social development, we believe, is based on a secure, just society based on high ethical values. The third national strategy, 2024-2030, sets goals related to social cohesion. That includes increasing the participation of women in leading positions by 30% and advancing innovative solutions to social challenges. As for our international efforts, we believe that enhancing social cohesion is based on inclusiveness and trust. This is a necessity, not only a goal. This approach increases the possibility to resist shocks and reduces opportunities used by extremists to dismantle societies. Important organizations in Qatar are making tireless efforts to fund initiatives that foster social cohesion. These initiatives address the root causes of conflicts to achieve just and durable peace. This is a sine qua non to achieve sustainable solutions to conflicts and to ensure regional and international stability. In this context, we stress the need to find a just settlement to the question of Palestine based on the two-state solutions as indicated by the New York Declaration emanating from the high level conference on the peaceful settlement of the question of Palestine and the implementation of the two-state solution last July. Qatar is hosting the second World Social Summit in 2025. It will be held in Doha in November. It is one of the most important events of this year. We're confident that this conference will provide a unique opportunity to mobilize support at the international level to address the urgent and complex challenges, to increase the resilience of societies, and to support international efforts to achieve sustainable peace. In conclusion, the state of Qatar is firmly committed to enhancing social cohesion and inclusive governments as two main pillars necessary for the development of societies, enhancing sustainable peace in the world. We believe the PBC is playing a vital role in this regard. I thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Chair, rather.
I thank the representative of Qatar and give now the floor to Her Excellency Hanna Liko, Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs of Austria, followed by Burkina Faso.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. At the heart of every peaceful society lies trust. Trust among citizens, trust in institutions, and trust that differences can be resolved through dialogue rather than violence. Where trust exists, communities show remarkable resilience even in the face of crisis. Without it, fragility and polarization take root. Strengthening social cohesion and inclusive governance is not an abstract goal, but a concrete necessity for preventing conflict and sustaining peace everywhere. It is also a call to action for all of us gathered here today. I would like to highlight three aspects in this regard. First, inclusive participation. Sustainable peace cannot be achieved without the voices of those who are too often marginalized. especially women and youth. The full, equal and meaningful participation in decision-making strengthens legitimacy, ensures that peace agreements reflect the needs of communities and contributes to reconciliation. Austria is firmly committed to advancing the women, peace and security agenda and to promoting the participation of youth as positive agents of change. Second, addressing the risks of climate change. Examples have shown how climate-induced livelihood disruptions can heighten communal tensions and be exploited by extremist groups. It is therefore essential to integrate climate adaptation and natural resource management into peacebuilding strategies. Austria stands ready to support efforts such as the work of the climate security mechanism that link environmental sustainability with conflict prevention and peacebuilding. We are doing so actively right now as co-chair of the Climate Security Mechanism Joint Steering Committee. Third, predictable financing for peacebuilding. The Peacebuilding Fund has proven its value by supporting national and local initiatives that build trust, whether through community reconciliation, youth empowerment, or inclusive governance. We commend the Fund's work that has been essential to stabilization and recovery and are honored to have contributed 1 million euro over the past two years. Austria will continue to advocate for more sustainable and adequate financing for the PBF and for peacebuilding activities more broadly. Austria firmly believes that social cohesion is not a byproduct of peace, it is its foundation. We will therefore remain a strong supporter of the Commission's efforts to strengthen inclusive governance, promote reconciliation, and foster community resilience. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Austria and will now give the floor to His Excellency Karamoko Jean-Marie Traore, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation, and Burkina Be Abroad of Burkina Faso.

Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of Burkina Faso, I wish to take this opportunity to thank the United Nations for this meeting dedicated to social cohesion and inclusive governance. Both are key for enhancing community-based resilience and building lasting peace. For nearly a decade, my country has been encountering numerous challenges and threats to terrorism, mass displacement of people, the consequences of climate change. These are challenges which have undermined our social fabric and imperiled our country's economy. And but our people are firmly convinced that it is important for them to take ownership of the destiny. More than 1 million IDPs managed to return to their homes in 2025, thanks to international solidarity and thanks to the patriotic commitment of the sons and daughters who have mobilized significant resources. This momentum demonstrates the dedication and sacrifice of our people, their commitment to building peace. We applaud the support from the PBF. Since 2017, the PBF has been supporting significant initiatives to boost community-based resilience and to bring in young people and women in peace and governance initiatives. A recent statement of Maram Bouimena, the founder of the Women for Dignity in Sahel, is a clear demonstration of this. Local voices are necessary for sustainable solutions. Chairman, to enhance the benefits, there's a need to finance direct and flexible financing specifically for countries of the Alliance of Sahel States. There is a need to invest in domestic local solutions by investments in local economies and traditional conflict resolution mechanisms. Three, the promotion of inclusive governance, which is respectful of the sovereignty of states and open to the meaningful participation of marginalized communities, women, and young people. Fourth, the adoption of an integrated approach which brings together social cohesion, climate adaptation, and prevention of violent extremism. Ladies and gentlemen, Burkina Faso, alongside fraternal countries Mali and Niger, we remain committed to transforming these challenges into opportunities. We are committed building a lasting peace based on social cohesion, based on justice, based on shared prosperity. Burkina Faso is open to building equitable partnerships, with respect for our choices and with a value being placed on local initiatives. We think that lasting solutions are those which take into account the will of the people themselves. Thank you.
Thank you, representative of Burkina Faso, and give the floor to His Excellency Armanata Nasir, Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia, followed by the Philippines.

Thank you, Chair. This year's Peacebuilding Architecture Review presents an opportunity to reflect on its effectiveness and renew our collective commitment to sustaining peace. Indonesia's own history shows that peacebuilding is not a single act, but a continuous process of fostering social cohesion and inclusivity. Cultivating trust between communities has been the foundation of our resilience, and today's theme could not be more relevant. To this end, allow me to highlight four points. First, lasting peace requires inclusive dialogue. As a diverse nation, Indonesia has learned that dialogue across communities and faith is a source of strength. Foreseeing this challenge, our founding father enshrined "Bhinneka Tunggal Ika" or "Unity in Diversity" as a guiding principle. more than just a slogan, this is a way of life. Reconciliation in Aceh and nationwide interfaith dialogue platforms shows how inclusion prevents tension and builds resilience. The UN could further strengthen such platform to encourage understanding among societies. Second, inclusive government is vital. Since our reform process in 1998, decentralization has enabled broader participation and ensured local government can address grievances directly. Also important is empowering women and youth is central to our nationwide action plan on countering violent extremism, strengthening communities against radicalization. Third, the Peacebuilding Commission and Fund must play a stronger role. The Commission should provide space for inclusive dialogue, while the Fund ensures timely support for reconciliation, governance, and empowerment. Strong political and financial support is essential to sustain peace. Finally, peacebuilding must adopt a broader challenge. Social cohesion efforts should integrate strategies addressing climate risk, violent extremism, and transnational pressure. Our disaster recovery experiences shows how solidarity across communities can reinforce resilience and trust in institution. Chair, Indonesia will remain a steadfast partner in the peacebuilding architecture review. Together, let us ensure this architecture is not only fit for purpose, but it fits for the future, delivering tangible resilience for communities worldwide. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the representative of Indonesia for his remarks and will now give the floor to Her Excellency, Helen de la Vega, Vice Minister of the Philippines, followed by CARICOM.

Excellencies, Peace is enshrined in the Philippine Constitution, and we take pride in our history of forging pathways to peace through inclusive dialogue, consensus building, and participatory approaches to community development. The decades-long peace process in the Philippine South was crowned with success with the establishment of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region of Muslim Mindanao, or BARMM, in 2019. Building and sustaining peace is deeply intertwined with our development policy, which underscores preventing violence through creating opportunities for people. The Philippine development plan pursues an inclusive, transparent, people-centered, and human rights-based peace and security policy. In this spirit, the Philippines supports the ongoing peacebuilding architecture review to help strengthen our peacebuilding tools. This includes assessing the effectiveness, coherence, and impact of the Peacebuilding Commission, the Peacebuilding Fund, and the Peacebuilding Support Office. Inclusive participation in peace processes and peacebuilding through the Women, Peace, and Security and the Youth, Peace, and Security agendas sustains and legitimizes peacebuilding efforts. Any peace-building architecture should be fit for purpose, cohesive and agile enough to effectively respond to conflicts and their root causes in a rapidly evolving global security landscape. Experience has taught the Philippines the value of country-led and country-owned solutions to address gaps, enhance collective responses to terrorism, and mobilize international support. The localization of peace through building national capacities and implementing results-oriented approaches, enhanced through international support, are vital in conflict prevention and peace-building efforts. Excellencies, we stand in solidarity with regions that continue to suffer from the specter of terrorism. The rise of violent extremism is compounded by external interventions, geopolitical competition, pastoral conflict, and other systemic drivers. As a trusted partner and a committed peacemaker, the Philippines firmly advocates for international collaboration underpinned by a rules-based order. We should strengthen multilateralism for the peaceful settlement of international disputes. We remain steadfast in our work toward narrowing development gaps, upholding the interlinked nature of the sustainable development goals, and empowering people in vulnerable situations, such as the youth, women, older persons, and migrants. As Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. stated, and I quote, "Peace is more than the cessation of hostilities. It is about the creation of a social order that values human dignity, improves lives, and promotes progress." Peace is totally achieved not when the sound of gunfire has ended, it is when the clamor for better lives have been met. The Philippines remains committed to engaging with partners at the national, regional and international levels to strengthen our cooperation in preventing and combating terrorism in all its forms. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

I thank the representative of the Philippines for her remarks and will now give the floor to Her Excellency Elizabeth Solomon, Assistant Secretary General for Foreign and Community Relations of CARICOM, followed by Serbia.

Chair and distinguished delegates, it's an honor to address the Peacebuilding Commission on the subject of promoting social cohesion and inclusive governance to foster community resilience and sustainable peace. And allow me, Chair, to endorse much of what has been said before, and particularly what was just said by the Philippines. The Caribbean community has a proud history of promoting international peace and security. an effort anchored by our region's declaration as a zone of peace in 2014. This framework is not a mere aspiration. It is a commitment to the international rule of law that has successfully sustained our region for decades and is a testament to the very principles we are discussing today. The work of this commission in supporting democratic processes and institutions is most important and more important than ever. particularly in a world where trust in democratic institutions is eroding. This trend is particularly alarming in the Caribbean, where recent UNDP data reveals an alarming decline in support for democracy and a high distrust in government amongst youth from the age of 16 to 25. This vulnerability makes our society susceptible to corrosive influences, including gang culture, which directly threatens the social cohesion and inclusive governance essential for sustainable peace. CARICOM's priorities align directly with those of the Peacebuilding Commission. We are focused on building community resilience and strengthening the national institutions essential for sustainable peace. To move forward effectively, we need a deeper analysis to better understand this evolution of distrust. By working together, we can develop strategies to reinforce our institutions and empower our communities, thereby protecting the democratic foundations that have sustained our region. Chair, this brings me to the most pressing peacebuilding challenge in our region, the unprecedented and deepening multidimensional crisis in Haiti. This is not only a national problem, but a regional one, with far-reaching social and security impacts. The breakdown of social cohesion and the collapse of inclusive governance have created a vacuum filled by armed gangs whose coordinated attacks have brought the state to the brink of collapse. But they remain strong. These groups have seized control of an estimated 90% of the capital, looting critical infrastructure, hospitals, and humanitarian aid sites. This violence has not only led to the displacement of 1.3 million people and acute food insecurity for nearly 50% of the population, but it has also fueled a cycle of retaliatory violence by self-defense groups, further fragmenting society. An important mandate of the Transitional Presidential Council for the return to constitutional government is the holding of elections, which will remain elusive if security conditions cannot provide a safe environment for voters. Despite efforts of the Multinational Security Support Mission and the Haitian National Police, the security situation remains dire. The mission has been severely understaffed, underfunded, and under-equipped. On the humanitarian front, the Haitian Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan is a dismal 12% funded, making it the least funded humanitarian response in the world. CARICOM, despite its limited resources, has consistently provided good offices and international advocacy. The CARICOM Eminent Persons Group has facilitated dialogue with Haitian stakeholders. the Transitional Presidential Council, and the international partners regarding the governance process and security issues. CARICOM leaders have also played an important role through international advocacy for urgent and necessary international action and resources to address the deepening crisis. We welcome the recent renewed consultations at the UN Security Council and the proposed gang suppression force, as well as the OAS-initiated, Haiti-led roadmap for stability and peace with regional and international support. Peacebuilding, as we know, requires more than just security. It means addressing the root causes of violence, strengthening the rule of law, and rooting out corrupt practices. Successful initiatives such as voluntary disarmament programs and social development projects can help rebuild the social fabric. Chair, social cohesion remains a key component of our deep belief in CARICOM in retaining the Caribbean as a zone of peace, and we welcome these and future opportunities to engage with the Peacebuilding Commission. I thank you, Chair.

I thank the representative of CARICOM for her remarks and give now the floor to Her Excellency, Ms. Nirvana Jovanovic, State Secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, followed by the United Kingdom.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honor to address you today on a topic that stands at the very heart of sustainable peace and international cooperation, promoting social cohesion and inclusive governance as the foundation of the resilient communities. In times of profound global uncertainty, our societies face overlapping challenges, geopolitical tensions, climate change, migration, inequality, and polarization. Each of these pressures can test the social fabric of our communities. But history teaches that peace is not simply the absence of conflict. It is the presence of trust, fairness, and shared belonging. Social cohesion is the glue that binds diverse individuals into a united society. It requires inclusive governance because when communities feel heard, represented, and respected, they become more resilient in the face of the crisis. We have seen that when governments prioritize dialogue, transparency, and participation, they build trust not only between citizens and institutions, but also among communities that may once have been divided. From a national perspective, Serbia attaches great importance to strengthening social cohesion and fostering inclusive governance. Building on the lessons of our own history, we remain committed to dialogue, cooperation, and reconciliation both within our society and in the wider region of the Western Balkans. We firmly believe that sustainable peace can only be achieved when all communities feel safe, represented, and respected. By promoting equal opportunities, protecting minority and engaging in constructive regional cooperation, Serbia contributes actively to regional stability, resilience, and lasting peace. At the same time, fostering social cohesion is not a task for governments alone. It requires strong international cooperation and joint efforts at the global level. No country can address these challenges in isolation. By strengthening multilateralism, sharing best practices, and supporting one another through international frameworks, we create the conditions in which inclusivity, stability, and peace can truly take root and endure. Excellencies, as we look ahead, let us reaffirm our shared commitment to a peace not only as a distant aspiration, but as a daily practice rooted in justice, inclusivity, and human dignity. Only together we can build resilient societies capable of withstanding the challenges of today and tomorrow. Let us choose cooperation over division, inclusion over exclusion, and peace over conflict. This is the responsibility we owe to our people and to future generations. I thank you.

I thank the representative of Serbia and give now the floor to Her Excellency the Right Honourable Baroness Jenny Chapman, Ministry of State for International Development, Latin America and the Caribbean of the United Kingdom, followed by Cambodia.

Thank you, Chair. The United Kingdom values the work of the Peace Building Commission and welcomes today's discussion. And thank you to today's briefers who have gone before me. Instability is rising and there are more conflicts than at any time since the middle of the last century. This hits the poorest and the most vulnerable hardest. The economic impact was $19 trillion last year alone, and we have to face up to reality. There are three things that we must do now. First, we must renew our approach to peacebuilding. The Secretary-General's UN80 Initiative and the Peacebuilding Architecture Review offer the best chance that we have to reshape how the UN supports countries in crisis. We need clearer links between decisions in New York and action on the ground. We need UN agencies working together. We need resident coordinators empowered to lead, all in support of governance that builds trust, resilience, and the meaningful and safe participation of women. Second, we all know we must do more to prevent conflict before it starts. For our part, the UK is investing in early warning systems and strategies for prevention led by local communities, empowering women and tackling the causes of extremism. And we must make national prevention central to how the UN sustains peace as well. So today, I'm pleased to announce the UK's voluntary contribution of over $7 million to the UN Peacebuilding Fund this year. And third, we need stronger partnerships to maximise impact. That includes the Peacebuilding Commission bringing together different parts of the UN and regional groups like the African Union. We also need the UN and international financial institutions to bring together political leadership and financial expertise. Finally, I want to restate that this urgent work cannot wait. We all know we have to do a better job to reverse the trend of rising conflict around the world. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United Kingdom and give now the floor to His Excellency Parit Khan, Secretary of State of the Kingdom of Cambodia, followed by the European Union.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, I'd also allow me to express Cambodia's deep appreciations to the leadership of Germany as this year's chair of Peacebuilding Commission for convening this important discussion on advancing social cohesions as a cornerstone of conflict prevention and peacebuilding. Cambodia align with the recognition in Secretary General recent report that division, whether political, ethnic, religious, or regional, remain among the most persistent driver of fragility and conflict. Where trust between people and institution is absent, grievance deepen, polarization grow, and society become vulnerable to manipulation by extremist actor. Mr. Chairman, in this connection, allow me to share Cambodian perspective on how social cohesion is built resilience is enhanced, and peace is maintained. First, reconciliation and inclusive governance are indispensable. Cambodian post-conflict recovery demonstrates this clearly. Our win-win policy, launched in the late 1990s, brought an end to three decades of civil conflict without further bloodshed. By guaranteeing security, safety, prosperity, and dignity for all factions upon reintegration. This policy restored trust, promoted national reconciliation, and laid a durable foundation for peace. Second, justice and accountability are fundamental to healing. With the strong support of the United Nations, the Extraordinary Chamber in the Court of Cambodia, ECCC, delivered a measure of justice to victims of the genocidal regime. This process, though difficult, was vital in addressing trauma, reinforcing national reconciliation, and strengthening the legitimacy of our institution. Third, peace can only be sustained through the inclusive development. Good government must be rooted in dignity and equal opportunity. Cambodia has pursued policy to ensure that women, youth, and indigenous people are represented across government structure and empowered in public life. At the same time, Expanding access to justice, social protection, and rural development, higher education and quality, and deliver tangible peace and deliver to our people. In closing, Cambodia's journey show that even the most fractured society can rebuild when reconciliation is prioritized, governance is inclusive, and partnership are strong. We reaffirm our steadfast commitment to working with our partner in this commission to promote social cohesion, strengthen resilience, and advance future founded on harmony, solidarity, and sustainable peace. I thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I thank the representative of Cambodia. I was informed that Olaf Schuck from the European Union has already left the room, so I give the floor to His Excellency Christopher Cutia, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Tourism of Malta as last speaker.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, strengthening social cohesion is fundamental to prevent violent conflict and sustaining peace. Around the world, we see how inclusive policies, resilient communities and responsive institutions can help societies overcome division and build lasting stability. From Malta's perspective, Experience has shown that investing in inclusive education, empowering local communities, and fostering intercultural dialogue are effective ways to prevent polarisation. And this is also in view of the phenomenon of a large expatriate community of particularly people coming from India and Italy to work in Malta. Community-led initiatives supported by strong and transparent institutions help to build trust and ensure that no one feels left behind. Inclusive governance is equally vital. In Malta, accessible institutions, empowered municipalities, and a strong legal framework that guarantees equality before the law help address grievances and reduce marginalization. By ensuring transparency, subsidiarity, protecting minority rights, and encouraging dialogue, we can reinforce the bond between communities and institutions. Amidst the current turbulent times, The Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund have a critical role to play in a number of different political contexts. They can promote dialogue, strengthen national institutions, and support reconciliation efforts that are rooted in local ownership. The PBF, in particular, provides catalytic support to community-based initiatives, while the PBC ensures sustained international engagement and mobilization of resources over time. In this regard, the current review of the peacebuilding architecture is therefore a key opportunity to ensure that both the PBC and the PBF are equipped to respond effectively to evolving peacebuilding needs. Malta supports a forward-looking review that enhances inclusivity, strengthens partnerships, and secures adequate, predictable financing. Finally, we must recognize that social cohesion cannot be pursued in isolation. Climate risks, violent extremism, and transnational challenges are deeply interconnected with peace and stability. Malta advocates for integrated approaches that are climate-sensitive, youth-centered, and responsive to today's global realities. By addressing these challenges together, we can renew trust, strengthen resilience, and ensure that peacebuilding efforts are both inclusive and sustainable. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Looking at the time and bearing in mind that we will need to conclude at 1:00 p.m. sharp, we will not be able to accommodate any further speakers. We encourage delegations who are unable to speak to share their statements with e-delegates so they may be included in the deliberations. Before concluding today's meeting, I would like to thank all of you, dear colleagues, for your valuable insights and contributions to today's discussion. In particular, I would like to thank our briefers for sharing the expertise and the national perspective with all of us. This is what the PBC is all about. Let me highlight some key takeaways from my point of view. First, we have seen that fostering social cohesion is an integral part of peacebuilding and sustaining peace. and crucial to ensure that peace is not imposed upon, but built from within societies. Second, the cooperation and collaboration between the United Nations, governments, and civil society organizations is instrumental for successful peacebuilding efforts. The Peacebuilding Commission, with its convening function, can play a hinge role, bringing stakeholders together, but also pooling resources and knowledge. Third, financing for peacebuilding remains one of the central challenges for peacebuilding and conflict prevention. Broadening the donor base of the Peacebuilding Fund and connecting the Peacebuilding Commission and the Fund through the interactive strategic dialogue, which we introduced this year, is an important step. Likewise, we need to continue building links along the humanitarian development peace nexus such as to the World Bank and other international financial institutions. Let me finish by emphasizing once again that the ongoing peacebuilding architecture review provides an important opportunity to ensure the peacebuilding architecture can fulfill its important mandate effectively. Let us all use this opportunity to collectively strengthen the peacebuilding architecture, ensuring that peacebuilding activities here in New York accompany meaningful action on the ground and support national peace building and conflict prevention efforts. I thank you. The session is now adjourned.
